title: Bit patterns and the life of an integer
summary: One bit pattern read as different types, reinterpreting bits with to_bits and transmute, integer ranges and overflow, two's complement, the checked, wrapping, saturating and overflowing families, bitwise operators and shifts, and endianness.

sections: PR ch3 Checked, Wrapping, Saturating, and Overflowing Arithmetic

blocks.md:
This chapter follows *Rust in Action*'s "Data in Depth": we open up the values you have been using and look at the bits. Knowing the representation explains overflow bugs, floating-point surprises and binary file formats, and it is the foundation for the low-level chapters that follow.

The first lesson is the most important: **a bit pattern has no meaning on its own. The type gives it meaning.** The same 16 bits are 50115 as a `u16` and -15421 as an `i16`:

blocks.explain: `{:016b}` formats as binary, padded with zeros to 16 places. The CPU stores exactly the same bits; only the type tells Rust how to interpret them.

blocks.title: Reinterpreting bits
blocks.md: You can ask Rust to treat one type's bits as another's. *Rust in Action* uses `std::mem::transmute`, the least safe function in the language: it copies bits between any two types of the same size, with no checks at all. For floats, the standard library has safe methods that do the same thing: **`f32::to_bits`** and **`f32::from_bits`**.

blocks.title: Text is bits too
blocks.md: A "text" file is a binary file that follows an **encoding**: a consistent mapping from bit patterns to characters, such as UTF-8. The same bytes interpreted with a different encoding become garbage. That is why Rust's `String` guarantees valid UTF-8 and `Vec<u8>` does not.

blocks.title: Ranges and overflow
blocks.md: An integer type has a fixed number of bits, so a fixed range. A `u16` has 2^16 = 65,536 patterns: 0 to 65,535. What happens at 65,535 + 1? There is no 17th bit. In a **debug** build Rust **panics** ("attempt to add with overflow"). In a **release** build (`cargo build --release`) the check is removed and the value **wraps around** to 0. When the compiler can see the overflow at compile time, it refuses to build:

error: this arithmetic operation will overflow

3 |     let c: u8 = a + b;
  |                 ^^^^^ attempt to compute `200_u8 + 200_u8`, which would overflow
  |

blocks.title: Two's complement: how i8 stores negative numbers

steps.title: The top bit has a negative weight
Negation is invert and add one
Addition needs no special case
steps.md: The CPU adds signed and unsigned numbers with the same circuit. `1111_1011` (-5) + `0000_0111` (7) = `1_0000_0010`; drop the carry and you get `0000_0010` = 2.

steps.title: Casting keeps the bits
steps.md: `-5i8 as u8` is 251: the bits `1111_1011` are reinterpreted, not converted. `as` between integers of different sizes truncates or extends them.

blocks.title: Choosing what overflow means
blocks.md: When overflow is possible, say what should happen. *Programming Rust* describes four method families on every integer type:

blocks.explain: `i8::MIN.abs()` has no answer: +128 does not fit in an `i8`. Two's complement has one more negative number than positive ones.

blocks.title: Bitwise operators and shifts
blocks.md: `&` (and), `|` (or), `^` (xor), `!` (not) work bit by bit; `<<` and `>>` shift. Together they let you pack several small values into one integer, test single bits and build **masks**: `x & 0b1111` keeps the lowest four bits, `(x >> 4) & 0xF` gets the next four. On signed types, `>>` copies the sign bit in (arithmetic shift). `count_ones`, `leading_zeros` and `rotate_left` are handy too.

blocks.title: Endianness
blocks.md: A `u32` takes four bytes. In which **order** are they stored? **Little-endian** machines (x86, most ARM) put the least significant byte first; **big-endian** puts the most significant first, and is the convention for network protocols ("network byte order"). Within your program you never notice, but as soon as bytes go to a file or a socket, the order must be agreed. Rust makes it explicit with `to_le_bytes`, `to_be_bytes`, `from_le_bytes` and `from_be_bytes`.

blocks.explain: `to_ne_bytes` uses the native order of the machine; this output comes from a little-endian computer.

blocks.title: Packing a date into 16 bits
blocks.md: The old FAT file system stores a date in a `u16`: bits 15–9 are the year minus 1980, bits 8–5 the month, bits 4–0 the day. Write `pack(y, m, d)` and `unpack(bits)` with shifts and masks.
hints: Shift each field to its position and combine with `|`: `((year - 1980) << 9) | (month << 5) | day`.
To read the month, shift right by 5 and keep 4 bits: `(bits >> 5) & 0b1111`.

blocks.title: Bit manipulation toolkit
blocks.goal: Work directly with bit patterns: two's complement, overflow policies, masks and byte order.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn to_binary_i8(x: i8) -> String`: the 8-bit two's complement pattern, e.g. `-5` → `"11111011"`.
- `pub fn negate_manually(x: i8) -> i8`: invert the bits and add one, with wrapping (so `i8::MIN` stays `i8::MIN`). Do not use unary `-`.
- `pub fn add_policy(a: u8, b: u8, policy: &str) -> Option<u8>`: `"checked"` (None on overflow), `"wrapping"`, `"saturating"`; any other policy → `None`.
- `pub fn set_bit(x: u32, n: u32) -> u32`, `pub fn clear_bit(x: u32, n: u32) -> u32`, `pub fn is_set(x: u32, n: u32) -> bool`.
- `pub fn swap_endian(x: u32) -> u32` without `swap_bytes`: build it from shifts and masks.
- `pub fn parse_be_u16s(bytes: &[u8]) -> Vec<u16>`: read pairs of bytes as big-endian `u16`s; ignore a trailing odd byte.
hints: `format!("{:08b}", x as u8)` prints the bits of an `i8`.
blocks.solution_explain: `x as u8` keeps the bits and changes only the interpretation, which is exactly what printing the pattern needs. `swap_endian` isolates each byte with a mask and moves it to the mirrored position.

points: A bit pattern means nothing without a type; to_bits/from_bits reinterpret safely, transmute unsafely.
Integers have fixed ranges: debug builds panic on overflow, release builds wrap.
Signed integers use two's complement: invert and add one to negate.
Pick an overflow policy with checked_, wrapping_, saturating_ or overflowing_ methods.
Masks and shifts pack and unpack fields; to_le_bytes/to_be_bytes fix the byte order.

terms.def: The raw sequence of bits stored in memory, which a type interprets.
A result outside the range of the integer type.
The encoding of signed integers in which the top bit has negative weight.
An integer used with & to keep or clear selected bits.
The order in which the bytes of a multi-byte value are stored: little-endian or big-endian.
std::mem::transmute, an unsafe function that reinterprets the bits of one type as another of the same size.
